This is called jargon, and technical jargon has existed as long as technical things have existed.
The reason jargon exists is to make the point far more concise.
I bet you even use some jargon yourself.
The purpose is not about sounding good or professional, but it's about making a point clear and understandable to those who already have a level of comprehension within the given technical field.
Different levels of tutorials do exist, and they often target different audiences. Obviously a tutorial for complete beginners who have only just launched a piece of software for the first time would feel intimidated by a large amount of jargon, meanwhile tutorials that teach more advance things may expect the user to already have a strong foundation of knowledge and therefore they can use jargon to make their point more clear.
What you may have discovered is your own personal learning preferences.
Everyone tends to learn things a little bit differently because our brains try to do it's best to connect new information to old information (the jargon for this is called assimilation, by the way).
The map of these brain connections is different in everyone and therefore...hooray learning preferences!

You are entitled to your opinion, but you are *not* entitled to free tutorials, so it would be a good idea to keep in mind that people are providing those to you even though they don't have to.
Some people might not have a lot of experience teaching others, and English might not even be their first language, but they still want to try to help the community, so they use their own time to try to share their knowledge. Getting "annoyed" because the free help that you're being offered isn't exactly how you want it to be is not a very good attitude. Nobody owes you any tutorials at all, let alone tutorials that are tailored to your wishes.
That being said, I do understand the sentiment that you're trying to express. But here are some better ways to handle it:
Leave some polite and constructive feedback to the tutorial creators, explaining which parts you had difficulty understanding, and why. Perhaps your feedback will help them figure out how to express things better in the future (assuming that the issue really is on their end).
Make your own tutorials, the way that you think they should be, and share them with the community. If the current situation "annoys" you so much, then why not do something about it?
CoolBeans said:
Maybe this is just an opinion, but I think it's a lot easier to learn when people talk using common terms, like "Player Tab" instead of "Actor Tab". Even something small like that will make a little bit more sense than, "Actors Tab"...
Click to expand...
Why would that make more sense? If the tab literally says "Actors", then calling it anything other than "Actors Tab" would likely be more confusing to just about anybody. Not to mention, "player" and "actor" are two distinct things within the engine, so trying to use the terms interchangeably will lead to issues when you try to get into more advanced stuff down the road.
Aside from that, if you don't learn the correct terminology now, then it will be harder to find help later. If you type a question into a search engine, you're unlikely to get useful results if you're using the wrong terminology. And how are you going to express your questions to other people, or understand their answers, if you don't know the right words?
I know you're not looking for life advice, but you will be doing yourself a huge favor if you try to assume that the people around you aren't idiots, and that they say and do things for a particular reason, and then try to figure out what that reason is. Even if it turns out that they *are* wrong, you will still almost always learn something in the process of trying to validate them. Looking down on everyone, with an unjustified sense of self-importance, will make it so much harder to learn things.

I like "professional talk." So here's how I would have worded this:
Permit me to articulate a particular vexation that plagues my cognitive tranquility: the propensity for individuals to engage in ostentatious linguistic exhibitionism, often masquerading as "professional talk." This practice entails the verbose and gratuitous articulation of concepts in a manner that obfuscates rather than elucidates, thereby rendering the information inaccessible to neophytes endeavoring to acquire proficiency in RPG Maker.
I intend no disparagement towards any individual; rather, I proffer this anecdote as an illustrative paradigm.
During my incipient foray into mastering the rudiments of RPG Maker MZ, I sought instructional guidance on the utilization of common events. I fortuitously encountered a tutorial by the esteemed "Drift Wood Gaming," whose exposition was characterized by simplicity, accuracy, and pragmatic exemplification. Conversely, upon subsequent engagement with a tutorial by "CazWolf" on an ostensibly identical subject matter—a topic with which I was already acquainted to a substantial degree—I found myself confounded by the labyrinthine explication.
It is my fervent supplication that individuals desist from endeavors to merely project an aura of erudition or professional gravitas, and instead strive for clarity and comprehensibility in their pedagogical endeavors.
Throughout my investigative odyssey, this very predilection for linguistic grandiosity significantly impeded my learning velocity. The prevalence of tutorials prioritizing rhetorical flourish over substantive clarity necessitated the consumption of multiple expositions on identical subjects prior to achieving any semblance of comprehension.

posts.author: Poryg
posts.body:
I have to disagree with those who say there is a right and wrong way to teach.
There 100% are wrong ways to teach. For instance, you ain't gonna learn anything from someone who teaches like mr. Mackey. M'kay?
But... We teach first graders math using numbers, while we teach preschoolers math using apples. If I go by the rule that "teaching people using incorrect terminology is wrong", this means teaching maths using apples is wrong. Yet we do it. Why? Because preschoolers aren't developed well enough to understand the abstract concept of numbers and it's much easier to give them examples and let them deduce the necessary knowledge from it.
We're adults, so we have no issue with understanding technical terms and as such, Caz's tutorials would be fine for  us. The OP is 13 according to the profile. A 13yo's capability to grasp technical concepts is going to be naturally lower than that of an adult. So it makes complete sense to teach a 13yo using terms they would understand if the circumstances permit it. I agree that using incorrect terms would suck in a book/manual. However, Driftwood's tutorials are video tutorials, so as long as you're not blind, you have the visual input in front of you. A kid will easily make the connection. If you don't, then maybe you're getting old
In conclusion, there is no "the" correct way of teaching. Any way that manages to get the point across with reasonable efficiency is correct and the way you will choose will vary depending on your target audience & the goals you want to achieve.
All that aside, as much as it surprises me that I'm playing the morality police, I want to ask both sides to calm down. OP, you say you "don't want to insult anybody", yet your language is bashful. If you don't want to insult anyone, don't use terms that have aggressive connotation like "blabbering" or you will risk people giving negative reaction.
And the other side, calm down. You've sent your point across, so resorting to mockery won't do anything other than potentially escalating the situation onto a fully fledged insult war.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
I honestly understand both points of view and... some of it has some weird conclusions drawn from it.
I have trained over 300 employees.  From the very young (16y.o.) to the very old (87y.o.) how to do a job.  I have taught savants and idiots.  I have taught people who have short-term memory issues.  Of everyone I ever trained, there were but two people who "didn't get it".
The first thought the job was "beneath her" and so had resolved herself to not learn it because it was a waste of time.
The second thought that "I was too high and mighty to be right".
The first lady wasn't even one of my employees and she quit after a week when she realized she wasn't going to get out of the training.
The second lady was a replacement for the Supervisor job I had left and she spent the next 3 years running that division into the ground, chasing off all the good employees, and ensuring that work across 2 divisions (my new one, and her own) was perpetually 30 business days behind (which is EXTREMELY BAD).
The second example is what will be relevant here.
When I teach someone, face to face, I use "real talk", like OP is suggesting.  It did not help as OP suggests it would (she still thought me too high and mighty, despite talking as if we were in high school and I was explaining things as quickly and simply as possible, with no jargon and no big words).
The problem, was her.  See, over the course of 3 years doing the job I was training her for, I had run my division out of work.  I had earned the respect and admiration of all my peers and nearly everyone in the office.  I was the "go to expert" for a large amount of problems and questions.  She had an inferiority complex.  My old employees would push back on her.  "No, that's wrong, Tai MT does things this way, it's the right way", "I'm just going to go ask Tai MT instead of listen to you, because he knows what he's doing", "You hire terrible employees, so I'm quitting".
She was 2 months into her 3 month training and immediately shut me out of training her any further.  She didn't come to me for help on anything.  She routinely put herself in situations where I was able to undermine her and her authority purely by answering a question or offering to help.
It got worse when she was asking other division to help get the numbers of days down she was, down, and I asked a simple question:  "What's the break even point?".  As in, how much work do you have to TODAY to stay as far behind as you are now?  Her answer?  "I don't now, I'll need other staff from other divisions to help us out before I can determine that".   This was in a public call.  I said "okay" and didn't push the issue.
I later sent her a private e-mail asking if I could speak with her.  I was going to teach her how to find "Break Even".  She decided the best course of action to this e-mail was not to "accept help", but to instead send a reply back to me that she didn't have time, there was no way she could figure out that information... and CC my boss... her boss... and the Director of the Department.
So, I stayed until 7 that night producing the document I had offered to teach her.  I compiled all the data, color coded it, made it presentable, and sent a "scathing but confused" tone e-mail back to everyone on the list.  It started with, "What do you mean you can't make one now?  Here's what I did for you..."
My document was then "mandatory" for her to that point to track staff productivity, and our Director praised me personally for creating it for them to use.  Mind you, I used to track all the information in the document IN MY HEAD and IN REAL TIME.
She forced me to burn that bridge with her.  Why?  Because she thought I was "too high above her" or some such.  Or, thought myself "too high and mighty".
Just as OP here is saying.  OP isn't knocking the information, they are knocking the PERCEIVED TONE of the tutorial.  They say so themselves.  They want tutorials that "put them on OP's level", rather than ones that "try to bring the OP up to the level of the tutorial giver".
What we're effectively dealing with is a problem of feeling inferior... which none of us can fix save for the OP.
It wouldn't be anything to just say, "not all tutorials work for everyone", and they don't.  Especially since most tutorials don't ask you to create something and are just, "let me show you" (which is hands-down, the worst way to learn, and most people's eyes glaze over when you do that, even with visual cues and information on hand, which is why I NEVER teach this way as it always produces as inferior trained person).  But. some people will prefer some kinds of tutorials to others.  Not a big a deal.
But, it's quite another thing to say, "I don't like this tutorial because it sounds professional and I am not".  That's a problem with an inferiority complex of some kind.  It's a mindset problem.  The problem is, in essence, "I refuse to learn from this person, because that make me feel like I don't know anything".  Very bad and dangerous mindset to have going forward in the world.
One wonders how OP feels about teachers in such a case.  How often they tune out in class or get unreasonably angry at them for "not acting like their equal" when they teach.
If someone knows more than you, they are superior to you on that subject.  Tough toenails in those cases.  You can either humble yourself and learn so you know as much as they do... or throw a temper tantrum and cry and scream and run grades, projects, and your work into the ground because "they didn't treat you like they were on equal footing with you".
There really aren't any options in between.

They actually do change these words in order to teach the child what the terms "addition" and "subtraction" mean. At the beginning, the question will not be
"If you have 4 apples and add/subtract 3, how many do you have?"
but
"If I give you 4 apples and you find another 3/eat 3, how many do you have?"
Once the child understands the terms "addition" and "subtraction", that's when apples turn into a visual aid. However, at the beginning nobody is "adding" and "subtracting", but "receiving", "buying" and "eating".
ATT_Turan said:
The apples, for a valid comparison, are the video. That's the supplemental aid.

Actually, no. Because what's primary information and supplemental aid is a tad different here.
When you teach abstract concepts, visual aid is useful to explain the stuff, but by itself is not enough to teach the concept. However, clicking the "Actors" tab is not an abstract concept. If you see it in a video tutorial, you'll follow the exact steps and you'll be able to do it even if you're completely deaf. As such, the video is the primary channel and the audio is supplementary. And we aren't teaching improper terminology. We're merely creating a bridge between a more technical term and sth a child might be more familiar with until the child becomes familiar with the proper term, similarly to "eating" and "buying" apples instead of "adding" and "subtracting".

posts.author: Avery
posts.body:
To get back to the "original problem" - if there is too much tech babble in the tutorials, you need to start with those tutorials, that introduce said terms. The help file for example, or one of the many many other very beginner friendly basics tutorials out there. Or press pause and google the term you are lacking. Or reread/repeat that part of the tutorial and see if you missed something.
As someone who
quite vividly writes tutorials
, there is just a certain level of expertise you have to expect the other person to have. While I try to give short explainations even for stuff I already explained in many other tutorials, you have to start
somewhere
. And once you are a little more experienced, you don't want to be explained all the basics on every single tutorial in depth.
And, general stuff aside, as an RM user, I expect you to be someone with a lot of agency: making a good game means you need to learn a huge amount of different skills to a certain level, walk paths that in that particular way maybe noone walked before and finish something.
You will face many situations where noone can spoonfeed you the solution and where you just have to research and learn to be able to bring your vision to life.
I personally started with RM as a teen, with a bare explaination of the basic functions by a friend of the same age, I remember how tricky it was to understand variables and switches (local and public) back then. But with much less resources for learning around back then, there was a lot of try and error and simply googleing and reading until I understood the things I tried to do. And without trying to sound like an old bloke who sits there with a raised digit and laments about "back in my days", a "can do attitude" and open mindedness about such problem brings you a long way. I am still the person who tells her boss "I have no idea if I can do that, but give me a day, I will try and I'll report back" and it usually works.
Tl,dr: This frustration doesn't help you, try to turn it into something positive. Ask kindly if someone can explain if you are really stuck, you might learn something and make friends. Research and try and get the positive experience of solving a problem. Broaden your knowledge along the way and become the skilled dev you want to be.
There might be bad tutorials out there, but I think Caz and Drifty do a good job as far as I've seen.

posts.author: Caz
posts.body:
Sorry for the small necropost but this thread only just came to my attention and I thought it'd be nice for people to have some perspective from the tutorial creators. Further blabbering incoming..
My tutorial series is intentionally as short as possible; each video comes in at 100 seconds or less (as is the name of the series). I'll acknowledge that style isn't for everyone, but it's for
me
. I hated watching tutorials where the person spends 30 minutes going "um, err, so" or dancing around a subject and taking up a lot of time. Some people love those tutorials though, and that's fine too!
It makes me happiest knowing that there are different materials out there to accommodate people's learning styles, because when I was 13, there was nothing available for someone like me who wanted videos that got straight to the point as concisely as possible.
So, as a few others have mentioned in this thread, I made my own. I wanted to be able to give back to people just like me who suffer with an atypical learning style. It's not meant to be for everybody, and that's okay with me. The beauty of the internet is that there are so many different types of videos out there now that you can just move on if you don't enjoy what you're seeing.
I do sometimes get comments about their speed, but the majority of them are from people who are grateful for the video style for the same reasons I enjoy them. So I'm sorry that they weren't to your taste, but there are many other free tutorials out there and I'm sure you'll find something that suits your needs too.
